Morsel
MOR-sel
noun
From the Old French morsel, a little bite, diminutive of mors, a bite, from Latin mordere, to bite; hence the smallest portion of food that can be handed to a man — and in Scripture, the measure of both hospitality and folly.

Biblical Definition

A morsel is a bite, a mouthful, the least portion of bread one man can offer another — and Scripture uses that smallness in three directions. First, as the modest word of hospitality. Abraham runs from his tent door to three strangers and says, “I will fetch a morsel of bread, and comfort ye your hearts” (Gen 18:5), and then sets before them a calf tender and good, with butter, milk, and three measures of fine meal — the promise small, the table large, which is the manner of true hospitality; and he entertained the Angel of the LORD unawares (Heb 13:2). Boaz says to the foreign widow gleaning in his field, “dip thy morsel in the vinegar” (Rut 2:14), and she ate and was sufficed and left some over. Second, as the measure of a quiet house against a quarrelsome one: “Better is a dry morsel, and quietness therewith, than an house full of sacrifices with strife” (Pro 17:1). Third, and terribly, as the price of a birthright: Esau, says the Holy Ghost, was a profane person, “who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright” (Heb 12:16). The word appears once more in the upper room, where the Lord dipped the sop and gave it to Judas Iscariot, and after the sop Satan entered into him (Joh 13:26-27) — the last morsel of covenant kindness offered to a traitor’s hand.

Webster 1828 Definition

A bite; a mouthful; a small piece of food. In Scripture the token of hospitality, the measure of a peaceable house, and the price Esau took.

MORSEL, a bite; a mouthful; a small piece of food; hence a small quantity of anything.

Old French morsel, diminutive of mors, a bite; Latin mordere, to bite.

Abraham’s morsel of bread to the three strangers (Gen 18:5).

Boaz to Ruth: dip thy morsel in the vinegar (Rut 2:14).

Better a dry morsel with quietness than a house of feasting with strife (Pro 17:1).

Key Scripture

Gen 18:5 — "And I will fetch a morsel of bread, and comfort ye your hearts; after that ye shall pass on: for therefore are ye come to your servant. And they said, So do, as thou hast said."

Rut 2:14 — "And Boaz said unto her, At mealtime come thou hither, and eat of the bread, and dip thy morsel in the vinegar. And she sat beside the reapers: and he reached her parched corn, and she did eat, and was sufficed, and left."

Pro 17:1 — "Better is a dry morsel, and quietness therewith, than an house full of sacrifices with strife."

Heb 12:16 — "Lest there be any fornicator, or profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright."

Modern Corruption

Hospitality has been outsourced to the restaurant and the church programme, and the morsel that once opened a home has been swallowed by a culture that makes eating an identity.

expand to see more

Two live misuses meet in this small word. The first is the death of household hospitality. Abraham’s morsel was fetched from his own tent by his own running feet; Boaz handed his own parched corn to a woman who had no claim on him; and the New Testament requires the same of every Christian house — given to hospitality (Rom 12:13), and of an elder, a lover of hospitality (Tit 1:8), and of all, use hospitality one to another without grudging (1Pe 4:9). What has replaced it is either the restaurant, where money buys company without covenant, or the church programme, where hospitality is delegated to a committee and a rota. Neither opens a door. The reason usually given is that the house is not fit to be seen, which turns hospitality into performance and then abolishes it; Scripture asked only for a morsel and a welcome. The second misuse is the elevation of the appetite: eating raised into a personality, the table made a stage, the meal made a moral statement. Pro 17:1 answers it in one line — a dry morsel with quietness is better than an house full of sacrifices with strife.

Recover the morsel at both ends, for the same word measures the highest kindness and the lowest bargain. At the highest: a bite of bread offered in the name of Christ is never small. He that receiveth you receiveth me, and a cup of cold water only, given to a disciple, shall in no wise lose its reward (Mat 10:40-42). Abraham did not know what he was entertaining, and neither do we. At the lowest: one morsel of meat is the recorded price of the birthright, and Hebrews sets it as a warning to a church, not to a pagan — look diligently lest any man fail of the grace of God, lest there be any profane person as Esau. And the darkest morsel of all was handed by the Lord Himself. He dipped the sop and gave it to Judas, an act of honour at an eastern table, the last kindness a traitor would ever receive from those hands; and Judas took the bread and went immediately out, and it was night. A morsel can be the beginning of communion or the last stroke of hardening. It is never neutral.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

A bite of bread; the token of hospitality, the measure of a quiet house, and the price of a birthright.

expand to see more

Morsel — Old French mors, a bite, from Latin mordere, to bite.

Hebrew path, a fragment or bit of bread (Gen 18:5; Rut 2:14; Pro 17:1).

Greek brosis, a thing eaten — one morsel of meat (Heb 12:16).

Promise small, table large: Abraham offers a morsel and sets on a calf and fine meal.

The sop in the upper room was a morsel of honour given to a traitor (Joh 13:26).

Usage

"Abraham promises a morsel and serves a feast — hospitality understates and overgives."

"Better a dry morsel with quietness than an house full of sacrifices with strife."

"One morsel of meat is the whole recorded price of a birthright."
